newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN WINE MAKERS WEIGH OPTIONS TO MEET DEMAND.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN WINE MAKERS WEIGH OPTIONS TO MEET DEMAND.

text.p: South African wine producers are considering expansion and foreign joint ventures to cope with continued strong export demand.
In their annual reports released this week, both Stellenbosch Farmers' Winery and Distillers Corporation said further growth was expected this year.

SFW said its export sales volumes had grown by 38 percent in volume over the last year and was expected to show continued growth for fruit juices and alcoholic fruit beverages as well as its traditional wine and spirit exports.
"In order to meet this expected increase, SFW will assess the potential of joint ventures with international partners," SFW managing director Frans Stroebel said.
He said SFW was now exporting to 50 countries, with Germany the largest market. Exports to Africa had grown "significantly", mainly to Kenya and Zimbabwe.

Distillers' managing director Jan Scannell said exports had risen 22 percent in volume and 46 percent in value to 84 million rand over the last year and this was expected to be maintained in the coming year.
To meet overall increased demand, Distillers had approved projects worth 47 million rand in the coming year, mainly to improve efficiency and quality assurance.
But both groups admitted that keeping up with increased demand was being made difficult by the shortage of natural and distilling wines.
Distillers Corporation chairman Boetie van Zyl said that the shortages were restricting growth in sales volumes.

"The prerequisite for successful competition in domestic and international markets is steady and prompt supply of quality products, as well as maintaining the correct balance between price and quality," he said.
This called for joint planning by the industry to ensure that the growing demand for South African wine was not jeopardized by stock shortages.
The new more liberal pricing policy in the industry, which replaced statutory minimum prices, would encourage producers to plant the cultivars needed for natural wines.

"The burden placed on the distilling wines and the domestic sales of brandy, to largely fund the stabilisation of the wine industry, will, however, have to be removed so that the natural incentive to produce sufficient quantities of distilling wines is not discouraged," Van Zyl said.
He criticised the high levels of excise duties imposed on wines and spirits in the 1996/97 budget while many imported products were evading excise duty, resulting in price instability.
